concept.name: Currency pair
concept.definition: The quotation convention of the foreign exchange market, in which an exchange rate expresses how much of one currency (the quote or counter currency) is needed to buy one unit of another (the base currency). Every FX transaction simultaneously buys one currency and sells the other, so currencies always trade in pairs; a pair quoted via a third country's market convention is a cross rate.
concept.intuition: You can never buy 'a currency' outright — you always pay for it with another currency, so every FX price is a ratio of two monies.
concept.mechanics: Pairs are quoted as base/quote (EUR/USD = 1.08 means one euro costs 1.08 U.S. dollars). The OTC forex market runs 24 hours through dealers and electronic platforms, with the major pairs (those including the U.S. dollar) the most liquid; changes in the rate reflect relative interest rates, flows, and macro conditions in the two currency areas.
concept.failure_modes: Quote conventions (direct vs. indirect) are a classic source of sign and inversion errors. Retail forex is typically highly leveraged, so small adverse moves can exceed the margin posted, and prices can gap over weekends when the market reopens.
concept.misconceptions: That buying EUR/USD acquires euros without selling anything — the position is simultaneously short dollars. Also, a rising pair does not mean the base currency 'strengthened' in isolation; the move is always relative.
concept.example: EUR/USD rises from 1.0800 to 1.0900: the euro has appreciated about 0.93% against the dollar, and each euro now buys one more U.S. cent.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
